title: docs(014): the Rahi realignment, adopted: 014 amends 001, 015's schema slice approved
body:

The Rahi realignment record and the specs that carry its work, with the owner's adoption of revision-4 rows ST-01 to ST-07 (2026-09-12) recorded in them. Spec text, `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` only: no code, no deploy input, nothing implemented.

- **014** (approved, `amends: 001`): the tree and the live plane checked against the handoff packet, the durable-state inventory, the declared-versus-enforced table, and the successor thesis. Section 4 is the only amending text; its 4.7 table names each 001 section amended, standing or replaced. Section 11 records every adopted row, where it landed, and what it supersedes in the revision-3 record.
- **015** (approved as the schema and pure-evaluator slice): the runner, job, lease and evidence-intake contract, with G-05 to G-10 written in (per-dimension verdict values with admission separate, trust only from independently supplied roots, typed byte references, device-grant runners, plane-returned lease timing). Schemas, fixtures and the evaluator live in statecraft-cli's Apache-2.0 workspace.
- **018** (new draft): the hosted service split out of 015, approvable only for the N=1 pilot after its prerequisites.
- **016** (draft): permits and the evidence chain, with a pilot slice and ST-07's deferrals.
- **017** (draft): the pilot cell (Part A, with Rahi's pilot checklist) before any migration of the live plane (Part B); factory and fleet preserved without expansion, retirement deferred.
- `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` state the adopted offer, reached through 014's `extends` edges (G-03).

One PR for 014 to 018 because the four drafts were authored and reconciled as one record, and the adoption changed all of them at once. Rows accountable to other repositories (G-11, G-02 and others) are cited, not recorded as adopted. Merging this deploys nothing: no Flux-applied path changes.

title: feat(013): adopt the spec-spine kit as the governed agent harness
body:
## Summary

Spec 013 claims the agent harness, which no spec owned until now: the session
protocol, the skills that carry a spec from "pick it" to "confirm the merge on
disk", the rules an agent may not violate, and the gate it passes before a
commit. The content is the spec-spine kit at the 0.18.0 floor, taken whole and
unedited; what is statecraft's is the project layer, which lives in `AGENTS.md`
so every `SKILL.md` stays byte-identical to the kit and a kit update is a copy
rather than a merge.

Ten skills (`prime`, `setup`, `next`, `build`, `verify`, `ship`, `shepherd`,
`spec`, plus `commit` and `code-review`) replace the previous five; the pre-kit
`/init` is removed rather than aliased. Four pipeline agents join statecraft's
own `encore-expert`. Four rules, three unconditional and one scoped to
`.derived/**`. The session hooks now read and never write. `Makefile` makes the
governed loop one command, and `make gate` is byte-identical to the kit's.

`spec-spine.toml` and `.github/workflows/spec-spine.yml` stay spec 000's
territory, reached by `extends` edges and cross-referenced by an amendment note
there. `standards/spec/` is claimed by 000 and refreshed to the 0.18.0 scaffold.
`.github/workflows/verify.yml`, the stack gate, is untouched.

## Four defects the adoption exposed

1. **The harness was never actually hashed.** Every glob in
   `[index] extra_hashed_inputs` ended in a bare `**`, which matches
   directories and contributes no bytes to any content hash. The skills,
   agents, rules, standards and workflows were nominally governed and actually
   were not, and the lint said so five times (`L-010`). Rewritten as `**/*`,
   with `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `Makefile`, `.githooks`, `.gitattributes` and
   `scripts` added.
2. **The committed registry was compiled by a v0.10.0 binary** at
   `specVersion 1.1.0`, against a 1.2.0 compiler. It stayed invisible because
   the session hook and CI both ran a writing `spec-spine compile`, so the
   drift repaired itself instead of being reported. Both halves now read
   through `spec-spine check`, and `[meta] required_version = ">=0.18.0"`
   refuses a binary below the floor: the coupling gate's bypass list is
   compiled into the binary, so two versions judge the same diff differently.
3. **`encore.gen` held ownership at 76.6 percent.** Encore's generated client
   surface is gitignored and rewritten by every build, so no spec can claim it,
   yet its 54 files sat in the coverage walk. Excluded from the resolver,
   coverage is 179 of 179 specifically claimed, so
   `[coupling] require_ownership = true` is turned on in the same change:
   `C-002` now refuses a changed source file that no spec claims.
4. **A record spec blocked the planner.** `001-statecraft-thesis` carried
   `implementation: pending`, so `registry plan` offered the thesis as ready
   work and reported specs 010 and 011 as blocked on a dependency that could
   never resolve. It moves to `n-a`, and the ready set becomes truthful: 010
   ready, 009 blocked on 010, 011 on 009.

## Testing

The gate as `AGENTS.md` lists it, all exit 0:

```
spec-spine check --fail-on-unresolved --fail-on-warn   registry fresh, index fresh
spec-spine lint --fail-on-warn                         0 errors, 0 warnings
spec-spine index coverage --fail-on-untraced           179/179, 0 floor-only, 0 unclaimed
spec-spine couple --base origin/main --head HEAD       36 paths checked, no drift
```

`make verify SPEC=013` passes all 17 commands of the spec's `## Verification`
block. `npm run typecheck` passes for the backend and the frontend. The stack
gate is unchanged by this branch and is left to `verify.yml`.

title: docs(009): record the fifth pin's live acceptance, and correct Finding 2
body:
Follow-up to #73, recording what the pin actually did in production.

## All three acceptance signals hold

1. **The roll.** Flux applied `main@5d29590`; the pod was replaced under `Recreate` with no intervention and came up `Ready` on `780eeefe`, zero restarts, edge 200.
2. **The clean stop and the clean boot after it.** A deliberate `kubectl delete pod` returned in **two seconds** instead of running the grace period out. The captured log carries `[entrypoint] received SIGTERM; stopping supervised processes`, then the entire chain SIGKILL used to cut off: rauthy's graceful shutdown, the app's `shutdown complete`, `RaftCore shutdown complete`, and twice (logs and logs_cache) `WAL writer Shutdown complete`. The replacement booted with **zero** `LockFile ... exists already` warnings, zero lock panics, zero restarts. First clean boot in this deploy's history.
3. **The index.** `fleet_app` now carries `idx_fleet_app_name`, on the image's first boot, exactly as spec 006 predicted.

Also records one intermediate worth not misreading: the *first* boot on `780eeefe` was still unclean, necessarily, since the pod it replaced ran the handler-less image and was SIGKILLed. The roll alone cannot demonstrate the fix; only the delete can.

## Correction to Finding 2

The 2026-07-25 amendment concluded the `Error creating backup: ... output file already exists` lines were upstream's to fix and would grow with `HQL_BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS` until every boot logged thirty. The diagnosis (raft log replay) was right; the conclusion was not.

The two boots above are a controlled comparison, same image, same data, same four retained backup files, consecutive:

| Boot | Preceding stop | Backup replay errors |
|---|---|---|
| `kp4dt` | SIGKILL (old image) | **4** (matching 4 files, within 160ms) |
| `zsblg` | handled SIGTERM | **0** |

Replay only happens when there is a log to replay, and an unclean stop is what leaves one. The noise was a second symptom of Finding 1, not an independent defect. The thirty-a-boot projection does not hold for normal operation, and the errors are now a *useful* signal: seeing them means the previous stop was not clean.

Local gate: `compile`, `index`, `lint --fail-on-warn`, `index check`, `couple` all green.

title: feat(009): pin the Deployment to the stop-handler image (fifth pin)
body:
## What

Moves the Deployment from digest `43717a27` to **`780eeefe`** (tag `7ff1347`, the PR #72 merge), and records the pin as spec 009's fifth-pin amendment.

## Why now

The 2026-07-25 fail-loud run closed section 5's oldest acceptance item, but it closed it by finding a defect: `docker/entrypoint.sh` is PID 1 and had no signal handler, so on every container stop rauthy was SIGKILLed and never released its hiqlite WAL and state-machine locks. Every boot after every restart began unclean, and intermittently the stale lock aborted rauthy into a crash loop, reachable from an ordinary `kubectl delete pod`.

The fix landed in PR #70 (and enrahitu #31), but the running image predates it. This pin is what makes that work real in production.

## What rides it

Two changes, from two specs' territory:

1. **Spec 002** (`docker/entrypoint.sh`): `TERM`/`INT` traps forward the stop to rauthy and the app, then wait. Installed immediately after rauthy is backgrounded, so a stop during the rauthy health wait is handled too.
2. **Spec 006** (`backend/fleet/*`): `fleet_app.name` keeps its index and loses `unique`; uniqueness is scoped to non-removed rows, enforced fleet-wide, and deploy answers a typed 409 ahead of the action gate.

## Risk

Lower than a pin normally carries. The `DROP CONSTRAINT` was applied to the live database on 2026-07-25 **ahead of** the #69 merge (precedent: the `port` `BIGINT` ALTER, third pin), so no ordering window exists, and since the deployed code has no name check at all that ALTER alone already fixed the production symptom. No schema delta, no secret delta, no env change. The digest change rolls the pod by itself under `Recreate`.

## Acceptance

Three signals, verified after Flux reconciles:

1. Rolled pod `Ready` on `780eeefe`, edge serves 200.
2. A deliberate `kubectl delete pod` logs `[entrypoint] received SIGTERM; stopping supervised processes`, and the replacement boots **without** the `LockFile ... exists already - this is not a clean start!` warnings every boot has carried until now. First time that absence is observable.
3. `fleet_app` carries `idx_fleet_app_name` (`ensureSchema` emits it only when the column is not unique, so it appears on this image's first boot, not on the boot after the ALTER).

Local gate: `compile`, `index`, `lint --fail-on-warn`, `index check`, `couple` all green (`couple`: 2 paths, no drift).

title: docs(006): say when the name index actually reappears
body:
A precision fix to yesterday's amendment, found by checking the live database rather than trusting what I wrote.

The amendment said `ensureSchema` creates `idx_fleet_app_name` "on the next boot". `createTableSql` emits the plain index only when the column is **not** unique, and the deployed image still carries `unique: true`, so the index appears on the first boot of an image built from this change, not on the next boot of the running pod.

Verified against production: the pod has booted twice since the `DROP CONSTRAINT` and `fleet_app` carries no index on `name` at all. Harmless (five rows, and the deployed code never queries by name), but this spec is the operational record, and a pending index that reads as a failed migration is exactly the confusion it exists to prevent.

Also records a consequence worth knowing because it inverts the usual order: **the ALTER alone already fixed the production symptom.** The deployed code has no name check, so with the constraint gone a re-placed name simply inserts and places. What the merged code adds on top is the typed 409 for a name that is genuinely still live, and that is the part waiting on the image.

Documentation only, no code. `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0, `couple` OK.

title: docs(006): stop claiming an invariant the name check does not enforce
body:
Two corrections from the automated review of #69. Both are about being honest in the record rather than about behavior, and both were fair catches.

## `liveHolder` overclaimed

The doc said "there is at most one live holder, because that is exactly what deploy checks before it places." The check and the insert are not atomic, so that is a property of the happy path, not an invariant the code or the schema enforces. A reader of `liveHolder` in isolation was being told something stronger than the code delivers.

It now says so, and says why returning the first row is still correct: every caller uses the result as an occupancy gate, not as an identity.

## The occupancy oracle was unstated

The spec amendment said the conflict does not disclose *which* tenant holds a name. It said nothing about disclosing that the name is held at all, which it does, fleet-wide, to any authenticated tenant willing to attempt a deploy.

Now stated plainly, with the argument for accepting it: `<name>.<FLEET_BASE_DOMAIN>` is public DNS with a public certificate, so occupancy is already observable by anyone without authenticating. The alternative (a false success that fails later in the cluster) would trade a disclosure DNS already makes for a silent failure, which is the wrong direction for this spec. Cheap enumeration is bounded by the tenant-write authorization the endpoint requires and by `apiRateLimit`, which `backend/fleet/encore.service.ts` mounts (verified, not assumed).

## Verification

No behavior change. Full suite 170 passed, `tsc --noEmit` clean, `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0, `couple` OK across 2 paths.

title: fix(002,009): forward container stop to rauthy; record the fail-loud run
body:
Two things that arrived together, because the second found the first.

## 1. The 009 fail-loud test ran, and passed

Section 5's oldest open acceptance item ("remove a required key, watch the crash loop, restore it") ran against the live control plane on 2026-07-25, deliberately, once.

`GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` was removed from the live pod Secret and the pod replaced. The same key the failed 2026-07-21 run used, so the results are directly comparable:

```
[required-env] GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET is empty or unset
[required-env] refusing to start; missing: GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET
```

exit code 1, `CrashLoopBackOff` within 33 seconds, edge serving 503. In 2026-07-21 the identical removal produced a **healthy pod and a silent 401**. The section 4.2 wrapper does exactly what it was built to do.

The method is recorded as carefully as the result, because the restore path is the reusable part: suspend the `secrets` Flux Kustomization so reconciliation cannot race the test, JSON-patch the key out, replace the pod by deleting it (never `rollout restart` on a Flux-managed Deployment), then **resume Flux so the restore comes from git rather than from anything typed by hand**. The restored value was byte-compared against the pre-test value before the local copy was destroyed. Deliberate downtime: about three minutes.

## 2. The recovery restart exposed a real defect

The recovery boot crash-looped three times on its own, on a pod replacement with nothing else wrong with it:

```
thread 'tokio-rt-worker' panicked at hiqlite-wal-0.14.0/src/log_store.rs:47:21:
LockFile /data/rauthy/db/logs is locked and in use by another process
```

`docker/entrypoint.sh` is PID 1 and had **no signal handler**. The runtime signals PID 1 and nothing else, so on every container stop the shell died alone and rauthy was SIGKILLed at the end of the grace period, never releasing its hiqlite WAL and state-machine locks. Every boot after every restart began unclean (three `LockFile ... exists already` warnings, present on the successful boot too), and intermittently a stale lock read as live aborts rauthy, which die-together turns into a crash loop.

Same failure shape as the seventeen-hour outage in §4.6 item 5, reached from an ordinary `kubectl delete pod`.

**The fix**: a handler forwarding SIGTERM/SIGINT to both children and waiting for them before exiting 0, armed right after `RAUTHY_PID` is assigned so a stop during the rauthy health wait is covered.

**The test**: `docker/entrypoint.test.ts`, the first test in this repo over `docker/`. It covers the *shipped* function rather than a copy: the `shutdown()` body is lifted out of `entrypoint.sh` by text and run against stub children, so editing the real function breaks the test. Verified in the other direction by hand: with the trap removed the harness exits 143 and neither child is signalled at all.

The same hunk lands upstream in enrahitu (its spec 007, statecrafting/enrahitu#31), so spec 002 records it as **convergent, not a fifth divergence** — a chassis entrypoint fix does not reach a stamped app through a pin, only through the next sync.

## 3. Diagnosed and deliberately not fixed

The recurring `Error creating backup: ... output file already exists` is **not a failing backup**. Backups are healthy: four consecutive daily files, no gaps. The errors are raft log replay: on boot hiqlite re-applies past `Backup` entries with their original timestamps, and the timestamp is the filename, so `VACUUM main INTO` hits a file that already exists. Four errors, matching the four retained files, all within 200ms of startup. Upstream carries the literal `TODO include a TS in the req to skip backups if they are replayed after a restart`.

This corrects my earlier "every few minutes" reading: it is once per boot, once per retained backup, and the E2E made it look periodic only because the pod was restarting more than expected (which finding 1 now explains). Not ours to fix: rauthy pins `hiqlite` from crates.io with its `[patch.crates-io]` block commented out, so the local fork is not in this image's dependency path. Worth an upstream issue; the one real cost is that it scales with `HQL_BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS` (30 here), so it will eventually bury a genuine backup failure.

## Verification

Full suite 174 passed (libsql + Postgres arms), `tsc --noEmit` clean, `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0, `couple` OK across 4 paths.

## Residual

The deployed image predates this handler. Closing finding 1 in production needs one image rebuild and digest re-pin, deliberately not improvised on the same night as the test.

title: fix(006): an app name is reserved by a live app, not by a row
body:
## The defect

`fleet_app.name` carried a database `UNIQUE` constraint, but `removed` is terminal and the row stays for the audit trail. So the first placement under a name retired that name permanently: re-placing it died inside the driver on `fleet_app_name_key` and surfaced as an untyped 500.

This was the residual finding from the 2026-07-24 in-pod E2E re-run, which had to place `echo2`/`cell2` rather than reuse `echo`/`cell`. Checked against the live database: the entire name pool used to date was already burnt (five rows, every one `removed`).

## The law

An app name is reserved by an app that **still exists**, not by a row that records one. `removed` is terminal and its cluster resources are gone with it, so the name returns to the pool while the journal keeps the history. Uniqueness is fleet-wide rather than per-tenant, because `<name>.<FLEET_BASE_DOMAIN>` is a single global DNS namespace.

## The change

- `entities.ts`: the column keeps its index, drops `unique`.
- `ops.ts`: `liveHolder`, a pure selector for the non-removed row carrying a name.
- `store.ts`: `findLiveAppByName`, fleet-wide, skipping removed rows.
- `api.ts`: `deploy` answers `APIError.alreadyExists` (409) when a live app holds the name. The check sits with the other request-shape rejections ahead of `gateOrDeny`, so no gate decision is spent on a request that cannot proceed, and the message does not disclose which tenant holds the name.

The check is application-level, not a constraint, so two simultaneous deploys of the same name can both pass it. Accepted rather than overlooked, and recorded in the spec: the correct constraint is a partial unique index (`WHERE status <> 'removed'`), which CoreLedger's schema layer does not express, and the cluster is the backstop either way (the second `placeApp` meets the first app's resources and fails loud into a journaled failed op).

## Verification

- `liveHolder` unit tests: name freed only when every carrying row is removed; a `failed` placement still holds its name (it can have left cluster objects behind).
- Persistence regression on **both** driver arms. Confirmed it bites: under the old schema both arms fail with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "fleet_app_name_key"`; under the new one they pass and `idx_fleet_app_name` replaces the unique constraint.
- Full suite 170 passed (libsql + Postgres arms), `tsc --noEmit` clean, `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0, `couple` OK across 7 paths.

## Live migration, already applied

CoreLedger schema init is CREATE-only and the spec 011 migration runner excludes destructive DDL by design ("write them by hand, review them"), so the live database needed:

```sql
ALTER TABLE "fleet_app" DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS "fleet_app_name_key";
```

Applied 2026-07-25 ahead of the merge (precedent: the `port` ALTER, 2026-07-23), so no deploy-ordering window exists. The five existing rows were unaffected. The plain `name` index is self-healing: `ensureSchema` creates `idx_fleet_app_name` on the next boot now that the column is no longer unique.

title: fix(006): pin @statecrafting/fleet-native 0.2.0, the per-app ingress allow
body:
## What

Bumps the `@statecrafting/fleet-native` pin from 0.1.0 to 0.2.0 and records the 2026-07-23 in-pod two-stage fleet E2E in spec 006 as a dated amendment.

The E2E placed two apps on two different ports in one tenant namespace (echo on 4000, the private enrahitu chassis on 8080) and surfaced the namespace-wide port pin: the addon's `fleet-allow-ingress-nginx` NetworkPolicy was namespace-scoped but pinned the deploying app's single port under create-or-tolerate-409, so the first app froze the allowed port set. The chassis rolled out Ready (kubelet probes bypass NetworkPolicy) and served 502 from the edge; the live policy was hand-patched to admit 8080 as mitigation.

fleet-native 0.2.0 (statecrafting spec 006 amendment, statecrafting/statecrafting#12) makes the ingress allow per-app (`fleet-allow-ingress-<app>`, podSelector on the app's selector labels, exactly the app's port) and `removeApp` deletes it with the app's other per-app resources. The napi surface is unchanged, so no `backend/fleet/` code moves; the spec amendment also records the operator residuals (the stale hand-patched policy to delete post-repin, and egress admitting only DNS + 443, so placed cells cannot reach SMTP).

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck`: clean.
- `npm test`: 147 passed, 18 skipped.
- `spec-spine compile / index / lint --fail-on-warn`: green, shards committed.

## Coupling waiver

Spec-Drift-Waiver: the substantive change is spec 006 territory (its amendment is in this PR); `package.json` and `package-lock.json` (owned by 002-app-shell) change only by the one-line dependency pin moving to the published 0.2.0, the same shared-surface shape PR #42 waived for the original repoint.

title: feat(006): deploy-chosen container port + FLEET_IMAGE_PULL_SECRET wiring
body:
## What

Two gaps blocked any real in-pod fleet placement of an enrahitu chassis image, surfaced while preparing the in-pod fleet E2E (the backlog item's own parenthetical: "pull secret, port 8080"):

1. **Deploy-chosen container port.** The addon's `DeploySpec.port` (default 4000) was never reachable from the HTTP API, while chassis images are fixed on 8080 (`EXPOSE 8080`, no `$PORT` in the entrypoint), so placing one would create every object and then hang at the 180s rollout wait on a probe aimed at a port nothing listens on. `DeployRequest` gains an optional `port` (integer 1-65535, default 4000 unchanged), persisted on `FleetApp` and forwarded on `update`, which rebuilds the Deployment spec and would otherwise silently revert a port-8080 app's probes to 4000 on its first image change. Exposed on `FleetAppView` and in the deploy attestation payload.

2. **`FLEET_IMAGE_PULL_SECRET` wiring.** Spec 009 §4.4 has always listed it as deploy-set, but the Deployment never set it, so `fleetImagePullSecret()` resolved empty in production and placed pods carried no `imagePullSecrets` at all: private images could not pull. The Deployment now sets it to `ghcr-pull`. The spec 010 catalog entry claimed a base64 dockerconfigjson derived from `GHCR_PAT`; no code ever read it that way (`fleet/config.ts` consumes a Secret NAME, and fleet's RBAC deliberately cannot create Secrets), so the entry is corrected (user-supplied, non-secret, still required) and `.env.example` regenerated.

## Operational notes

- **Live DB migration required before the image carrying this deploys** (CoreLedger schema init is CREATE-only): `ALTER TABLE "fleet_app" ADD COLUMN "port" BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 4000;` (precedent: the spec 011 `user_account` ALTER, 2026-07-22).
- The pull Secret itself is operator-provisioned per tenant namespace (fleet RBAC grants nothing on `secrets`); nothing automates that yet.
- The operator `.env` value for `FLEET_IMAGE_PULL_SECRET` predates the catalog correction and should be updated to the Secret name (`ghcr-pull`).
- The governance UI DeployForm does not expose `port` yet; follow-up under spec 007 territory if wanted.

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck` clean; full vitest run 25 files / 144 passed (18 skipped Postgres arms).
- `secrets:validate` (37 keys) and `secrets:check` green.
- `spec-spine compile/index/lint` clean; `couple` OK, 10 paths, no drift. Specs 006/009/010 amended in the same change.

title: feat(009): AI review CI port + fail-loud required-env assertion
body:
## What

Closes the build halves of two spec 009 tail items.

**1. `ai-pr-review.yml` + `ai-changelog.yml` (spec 009 §4.9).** Ported from OAP spec 085 and stripped to this repo's shape:

- Kept: stdin-fed diff (contributor content is never shell-evaluated), pinned `CLAUDE_CLI_VERSION`, draft-PR skip, `DIFF_SIZE_CAP` with a visible skip comment, API-failure classification (auth failures fail the job; API outages pass with a loud posted notice), retrying comment posts.
- Dropped: OAP's `workflow_call` orchestration (no `ci.yml` here; the trigger is plain `pull_request`) and the Local-Review-Evidence verifier mode (this repo's `/ship` posts no evidence comment, and dead trust plumbing reads as configured).

title: fix(002): strip Sec-Fetch-* in the rauthy proxy so upstream login works
body:
## The bug (found by a real login)

A GitHub sign-in reached the authorize screen, `bartekus` authorized, and the
browser was redirected to `app.statecraft.ing/auth/v1/providers/callback?code=...&state=...`
which returned:

```json
{"error":"BadRequest","message":"cross-origin request forbidden for this resource"}
```

## Root cause (confirmed, not inferred)

`backend/idp/proxy.ts` streams `/auth/*` to the loopback rauthy via undici
`fetch()`. **undici unconditionally rewrites `Sec-Fetch-Mode` to `cors`** (a
`fetch()` call always stamps its own request mode over any value passed).

Proven with a local undici test: sending `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate`, the server
received `cors`. And live against the deployed pod:

| Sent through proxy | rauthy result |
|---|---|
| `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` + `Mode: navigate` + `Dest: document` | **400** |
| no `Sec-Fetch` headers | **200** |

rauthy's CSRF guard (`csrf_protection.rs`, confirmed against 0.36.0 = the
deployed image) allows a cross-site top-level `navigate` but blocks a cross-site
`cors`, and `/auth/v1/providers/callback` is **not** on its path-exception list.
So the mode rewrite turns GitHub's legitimate callback navigation into a forged
`cors` request in rauthy's eyes, and it blocks it.

## The fix

The proxy drops every `sec-fetch-*` request header. It cannot forward
`Sec-Fetch-Mode` faithfully through undici, and a corrupted value is worse than
none: absent, rauthy takes its header-absent path and relies on the CSRF
defenses this proxy does not touch (the OAuth `state` parameter, PKCE, and
`__Host-` SameSite cookies). The live data above shows the header-absent path
returns 200.

Security note: rauthy's Sec-Fetch layer was **net-negative behind this proxy**
already, since every forwarded request arrived as `cors` and only ever produced
false-positive blocks. This removes that false signal; it does not remove real
CSRF protection.

## Divergence

Fifth divergence from enrahitu's chassis, and the first in app source rather
than the entrypoint, so it is baked into the image and needs a rebuild. Same
upstream-mirror follow-up as the other four: any enrahitu app that fronts rauthy
with this proxy and uses an upstream provider hits this.

## Verification

- undici mode-rewrite reproduced locally; rauthy version matched to 0.36.0.
- Live proxy behavior tabulated above.
- `compile`, `index`, `lint` clean; `couple` no drift.

Deploy needs a rebuilt image + digest re-pin (dispatched alongside this PR).

title: docs(009): fail-loud does not hold; the metadata.cloud line is not enough
body:
The deliberate fail-loud test that section 5 asks for was run live, and it
**disproved** the mechanism section 4.2 called "the single highest-value line in
the deployed config." Recording the result truthfully rather than editing the
spec to pretend it passed.

## The test

With `cloud: hetzner` in effect (the runtime logs `CLOUD_UNSPECIFIED`, so the
non-local resolution the spec wanted is active), on the live cluster:

1. Removed `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` from the pod Secret; rolled the pod.
2. Pod came up **healthy** (0 restarts, `GET /` 200).
3. `POST /github/webhook` returned **`401 invalid signature`**, not a crash and
   not `500 secret ... is not set`.

The resolver returned an empty string and the service verified signatures
against it, rejecting every webhook. That is exactly the silent-empty
degradation section 4.2 claimed `cloud != local` had abolished.

Fully reversed afterward: Secret restored to nine keys, pod healthy,
`/github/webhook` back to its `401` baseline, `GET /` 200.

## Why the premise was wrong

All eleven secrets are declared in `infra.config.json` as `{"$env": "<NAME>"}`,
and section 2.2 deliberately keeps every declaration. So a secret is **never
"absent from the runtime config"** (the condition that arms the throw). An unset
env var makes the `$env` reference resolve to empty, which is "configured to
empty," not "not set." `metadata.cloud` governs genuinely unconfigured secrets
(the twelfth, `GovernanceAnchorKey`, with no `$env` binding, is the one that
would actually throw), not the nine this deploy delivers. `fromSecretOrEnv` then
trims the empty value and falls through to an equally empty `process.env`.

A second correction rides along: these secrets resolve **lazily** in per-request
getters, so a missing one does not crash-loop the pod at boot at all. It yields
a healthy pod that fails only when the owning endpoint is first hit. Section 5's
"crash-loops the pod" was wrong on both counts.

## Why this matters

**A forgotten or misspelled secret degrades this platform silently today.** For
the webhook that means rejecting every delivery; for other secrets it means
proceeding with an empty credential. This is a real open gap, not a formality.

The fix is an explicit non-empty startup assertion over the nine required
secrets (the shape `scripts/verify-born-with.mjs` already uses), which fails
closed regardless of Encore's `$env` behavior. That is a chassis-or-app change
with an owner to assign, named as a recommendation and left to the spec that
owns the startup path rather than improvised into a manifest.

## Changes

- Section 4.2: the tested result, the `$env` root cause, and the recommendation.
- Section 5 + 5.1: the acceptance item marked tested-and-not-met, with both
  wording errors corrected.
- Coherence guard honored: the spec is corrected to match verified reality, not
  bent to keep a claim green.

Gates: `compile`, `index`, `lint` clean; `couple` no drift.

`relay()` and only speaks STARTTLS when `starttls_only` is set, so without this
variable port 587 is unusable.

**The manifest (spec 009):** re-pins to the image carrying that change (digest
`baf41728`, built from `2e3c9d7`, verified by grepping the entrypoint out of the
published image) and sets the SMTP env to **587 + `SMTP_STARTTLS_ONLY=true`**.

Why not 465, the natural first guess: Hetzner blocks outbound 465 and 25 from
the cluster (verified from a pod: 465 BLOCKED, 587 OPEN, 25 BLOCKED, 443 OPEN),
and getting SMTP wrong is an outage, not a lost feature: rauthy panics on an
unreachable mailer and die-together takes the app with it. This is exactly what
crash-looped the platform ~50 minutes after the 465 rollout looked healthy.

Section 4.8 item 1 now records the whole arc (closed → reopened on the egress
finding → re-closed here). The section 4.4 SMTP text, which had accreted three
contradictory same-day edits, is consolidated into one statement.

## Restore rehearsed (checkpoint 7 closed)

A Job restored the latest restic snapshot into scratch space, **never touching
`/data`**, and verified every piece of identity material present and readable:

```
OK   keys/access-private.pem (1704 bytes)
OK   keys/refresh-private.pem (1704 bytes)
OK   keys/rauthy-client-secret (64 bytes)
OK   rauthy/admin-password (24 bytes)
OK   rauthy/secrets.env (351 bytes)
OK   rauthy/db/state_machine (7 files)
REHEARSAL PASSED: snapshot is a restorable identity plane
```

A snapshot is now known to be restorable, not merely stored. That is the half of
checkpoint 7 a snapshot alone never proved.

## Checkpoint 6 unblocked

With mail delivering, the enrolment and MFA-verification messages a named
break-glass account needs can be sent. The rotation itself stays operator work,
so custody remains the generated password on the volume until it is done.

## A finding this PR does not act on

`fromSecretOrEnv` (`backend/tenants/config.ts:37`, `backend/fleet/config.ts:57`)
resolves each secret inside a per-request getter, so all nine required secrets
are resolved **lazily**, none at boot. That means the section 4.2 / section 5
acceptance framing that "removing a required key crash-loops the pod" is
inaccurate for these secrets: removing one yields a healthy pod that fails loud
only when the owning endpoint is first hit. The fail-loud mechanism is intact
(with `cloud: hetzner` the resolver throws before the env-fallback runs), but
where it fires is call-time, not boot-time. Flagged here; the deliberate
verification and any spec-wording fix are a follow-up.

## Verification

- Digest and `SMTP_STARTTLS_ONLY` confirmed inside the published image.
- Egress ports tested from inside the cluster.
- Restore verified against the live bucket into throwaway scratch.
- `compile`, `index`, `lint` clean; `couple` no drift.
